title: Mistake
subtitle: Common mistake, unilateral mistake, and mistaken identity
objectives: Explain when common mistake as to the existence or quality of the subject matter can render a contract void, and why the doctrine is now extremely narrow
Distinguish unilateral mistake as to a term of the contract from a mere mistaken assumption, and apply the objective test for knowledge
Explain why mistaken identity produces sharply different outcomes in face-to-face dealings compared with written or distance dealings

leadingAuthorities.role: Common mistake as to quality will only void a contract if it is fundamental enough to make the subject matter essentially different

leadingAuthorities.citation: Great Peace Shipping v Tsavliris [2002] EWCA Civ 1407
leadingAuthorities.role: Confirms and narrows Bell v Lever Bros; rejects a separate, broader equitable jurisdiction to rescind for common mistake
The objective test: a party's actual undisclosed intention is irrelevant if their words and conduct reasonably conveyed agreement

leadingAuthorities.citation: Hartog v Colin & Shields [1939] 3 All ER 566
leadingAuthorities.role: A buyer cannot snap up an offer they knew, or must have known, was a slip as to price
In written dealings, the contract is presumed to be with the named party on the document, not the party physically present

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Mistake is a small doctrine with a reputation for being bigger than it is. Most exam traps here are about spotting that a fact pattern is really a mistaken assumption dressed up as a mistake, or a common mistake claim that Great Peace has effectively closed off.

profileHooks.weakApplication: The test pool leans on scenario questions that ask you to sort a genuine mistake from an ordinary bad bargain — that distinction, not the case names, is what actually gets tested.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Read Parts 1 and 2 carefully before moving on — Bell v Lever Bros and Great Peace are doing most of the conceptual work for the whole lesson, and the rest builds directly on them.

overview.hook: Two shipping agents each fix the same stricken vessel's position, negotiate a salvage contract by reference to it, and only afterwards discover the ship was already thirty-five miles away, near enough to another salvage tug that the whole deal was pointless from the start. Nobody was lying. Nobody was careless in any way the law cares about. So was there ever a contract at all?

parts.heading: The case for saying mistake almost never applies
parts.voice: argumentative — makes the strongest case for a narrow doctrine, then locates the crack in it
body: Start from a position of real suspicion towards this whole topic, because the courts do. Contract law wants deals to stick. Every contract carries risk that one party's assumptions will turn out wrong, and if 'I was mistaken about something important' were enough to escape a bad bargain, no contract would ever be safe. Mistake exists as a doctrine, but it is deliberately built to almost never succeed.

Common mistake is the paradigm case: both parties share the same false assumption about some fact underlying the contract. Bell v Lever Bros is the foundational authority, and it is worth knowing that the claim in that very case failed — a company paid two directors large severance sums, not knowing that both directors had committed breaches that would have justified dismissal without any payment at all. The House of Lords held this mistake, serious as it was, did not void the contract: the subject matter (a severance agreement) was not essentially different from what the parties believed it to be, merely worth less than they thought.

That failure is the whole lesson in miniature. For common mistake to void a contract, the mistake must go to something so fundamental that the thing contracted for is essentially and radically different from what both parties believed — not merely less valuable, less useful, or a worse deal than expected. Getting a bad bargain because of a shared false assumption is not, by itself, a legal mistake at all; it is simply risk, and risk sits with the parties unless the contract says otherwise.

components.definition: A mistake shared by both parties as to an existing fact fundamental to the contract, at the time of contracting. It renders the contract void only where the mistake makes the subject matter essentially and radically different from what both parties believed it to be — not merely worth less.

interaction.prompt: In Bell v Lever Bros, why did the severance agreement remain valid despite the shared mistake about the directors' misconduct?
options: Because the mistake made the agreement a worse bargain, not a fundamentally different thing from what the parties believed they were making
Because one of the parties had acted fraudulently, which bars a mistake claim entirely
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right — the agreement they got was still, in substance, a severance agreement; it was simply a bad one given what was later discovered. That's a bad bargain, not a fundamental mistake.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: There's no fraud on these facts — the directors didn't know their conduct was disclosable in this sense either, at least not on the House of Lords' analysis. The real reason is narrower: the contract they made was still, in kind, the contract they thought they were making; it just turned out to be worth less.

parts.heading: Great Peace closes the back door
parts.voice: conversational — walks the reader through the case like thinking aloud
body: For decades after Bell v Lever Bros, there was a live argument that equity offered a second, more generous route to relief — a broader jurisdiction to rescind a contract for common mistake even where the common law test wasn't met, based on a Court of Appeal case called Solle v Butcher. That gave courts a kind of safety valve: even if the mistake wasn't fundamental enough to void the contract outright, a judge could still unwind it if fairness seemed to demand it.

Great Peace Shipping v Tsavliris shut that door. The facts are the ones in this lesson's opening: a salvage contract fixed by reference to a vessel's position, which both parties believed to be close to the stricken ship, when in reality it was far enough away that the contract's whole purpose was undermined. Even on facts that sympathetic, the Court of Appeal held there is only one doctrine of common mistake — the narrow common law one from Bell v Lever Bros — and no separate, more flexible equitable jurisdiction sitting alongside it.

So where does that leave quality mistakes today? Technically alive, but vanishingly narrow. The mistake has to render the subject matter something essentially different in kind, not merely disappointing in value or usefulness. In practice, this means most 'we were both wrong about something important' arguments now fail outright — parties are expected to allocate that risk through the contract itself, or simply bear it.

components.factsShort: Both parties believed a salvage vessel was close to a stricken ship and contracted on that basis; it was in fact around thirty-five miles away, undermining the point of the contract.
components.ratioShort: There is a single doctrine of common mistake at common law (from Bell v Lever Bros); there is no separate, broader equitable jurisdiction to rescind for a less-than-fundamental common mistake.

expanded.facts: The defendants needed a vessel to stand by a stricken ship for salvage purposes and, believing (on the claimant's own representation) that the claimant's vessel, the Great Peace, was in close proximity, contracted for its services. In fact the Great Peace was around thirty-five miles away — far enough that another, closer vessel would have been a far more sensible choice, and once the defendants discovered the true position they sought to cancel the contract, relying on common mistake.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Court of Appeal reviewed Solle v Butcher and the equitable jurisdiction it was said to support, and concluded that jurisdiction could not be reconciled with Bell v Lever Bros and should no longer be treated as good law. The correct test for common mistake remains that stated in Bell v Lever Bros: was the mistake sufficiently fundamental to render the subject matter of the contract essentially and radically different from what the parties believed it to be?
expanded.significance: This is the modern law: it collapses what had been treated as two possible routes to relief for common mistake into one narrow common law test, and confirms that a merely disappointing or less advantageous contract, however sympathetic the facts, is not enough.

interaction.prompt: In this extract, highlight the sentence that states the test Great Peace confirms for common mistake.
interaction.passage: The Court of Appeal held that the supposed equitable jurisdiction to rescind for common mistake could not stand alongside Bell v Lever Bros. The correct test remains whether the mistake is sufficiently fundamental to render the subject matter of the contract essentially and radically different from what the parties believed it to be. A contract that is simply a worse bargain than expected does not meet that test.
interaction.ratioSentence: The correct test remains whether the mistake is sufficiently fundamental to render the subject matter of the contract essentially and radically different from what the parties believed it to be.

parts.heading: When one party alone is mistaken about a term
parts.voice: dry and instructive — sets the objective test up as the tool that resolves everything
body: Unilateral mistake is a different animal from common mistake, and students frequently blur the two. Here only one party is mistaken — and critically, the mistake this doctrine cares about is a mistake as to a term of the contract itself (most often price or subject matter), known or reasonably apparent to the other party, not a mistaken assumption about some background fact that both, or even just one, party happens to hold.

The governing test is objective, and Smith v Hughes states it cleanly: what matters is not what a party secretly believed, but what a reasonable person would understand from their words and conduct. If your outward conduct reasonably conveys agreement to the terms as the other side understands them, you are bound by that agreement even if you privately meant something else — the law does not go rummaging in your head for undisclosed intentions.

Hartog v Colin & Shields shows the doctrine's actual bite. A seller of hare skins meant to quote a price per piece but, by mistake, quoted it per pound — a figure roughly a third of what was intended, wildly out of line with market practice and with the parties' own prior negotiations. The buyer tried to accept at the mistaken price. The court held no contract existed at that price: the buyer knew, or a reasonable person in the buyer's position must have known, this was a slip, not a genuine offer — and a party cannot 'snap up' an offer they know does not represent what the other side actually intended.

The line to hold onto: knowledge (actual or constructive) of the other party's mistake as to a term is what unlocks this doctrine. Simply getting a great, suspiciously good deal is not enough on its own — the question is always whether the offeree knew, or should reasonably have realised, that the terms didn't reflect the offeror's real intention.

components.definition: A mistake by one party about a term of the contract (typically price), of which the other party has actual or constructive knowledge. It prevents a contract forming on the mistaken term, because the objective test of agreement is not satisfied once the offeree knows the outward appearance does not reflect the offeror's real intention.

components.citation: Smith v Hughes (1871) LR 6 QB 597 — the objective test, stated as principle
components.text: If, whatever a man's real intention may be, he so conducts himself that a reasonable man would believe that he was assenting to the terms proposed by the other party, and that other party upon that belief enters into the contract with him, the man thus conducting himself would be equally bound as if he had intended to agree to the other party's terms.
elements: Outward words and conduct, judged objectively
A reasonable person's understanding of assent
The other party's reliance on that understanding

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that would most likely fix the buyer with the knowledge needed for a Hartog-style unilateral mistake claim.
interaction.scenarioText: A supplier's usual price for a batch of machine parts is around £4,000, agreed in earlier phone calls. Their written quote, sent the next morning, mistakenly states £400 due to a typing error. The buyer, who was on the earlier calls and knows the usual figure, emails back within the hour accepting at £400 before the supplier can correct it.
tappableSpans: usual price for a batch of machine parts is around £4,000
mistakenly states £400 due to a typing error
emails back within the hour accepting
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right — the buyer's own knowledge of the figure discussed on the earlier calls is what makes the £400 quote an obvious slip to a reasonable person in the buyer's position, exactly as in Hartog.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The typo itself is the mistake, but what matters for the doctrine is what the buyer knew or should have realised. The prior calls establishing the real figure are what fix the buyer with that knowledge.

parts.heading: Mistaken identity: the face-to-face problem
parts.voice: dialectic — sets up a tension between two lines of authority and resolves it
body: Mistaken identity sits at the collision point of two competing instincts. On one hand, if a rogue tricks a seller into thinking they are someone else — a person of good credit, say — the seller plainly did not intend to contract with the rogue. On the other hand, an innocent third party (often a finance company or a later buyer) may have acquired the goods in good faith, and someone has to bear the rogue's fraud. The doctrine's job is to decide which of those two innocents loses.

Smith v Hughes' objective test is the background principle here too, but identity cases add a wrinkle: the law has drawn a sharp line between dealings conducted face to face and dealings conducted in writing or at a distance. Where parties deal face to face, there is a strong presumption that the seller intends to deal with the person physically in front of them, whoever that person claims to be. On that presumption, the contract is usually only voidable for fraud, not void for mistake — meaning it is valid until the seller takes steps to rescind it, and a good-faith third party who buys the goods before that happens can get good title.

Written and distance dealings work the other way. Shogun Finance v Hudson concerned a rogue who obtained a car on hire purchase by presenting a stolen driving licence and signing the agreement in the real cardholder's name. The House of Lords (by a majority) held that where a contract is in writing, the identity of the contracting party is determined by the document itself: the finance company intended to contract with the person named on the agreement, not with the rogue physically present, so the contract was void for mistake from the outset. Because it was void, not merely voidable, no title could ever pass to a later innocent buyer of the car.

components.title: Mistaken identity — which rule applies?
components.description: A decision path for classifying identity mistake cases by the mode of dealing.

nodes.label: Did the parties deal face to face?
Yes → strong presumption of intent to deal with the person present; contract voidable for fraud, not void
No (written/distance dealing) → identity fixed by the document; contract void for mistake if the named party differs from the rogue
Void → no title can pass to any later innocent third party
Voidable → valid until rescinded; a good-faith third party who buys before rescission gets good title

components.textAlternative: If parties deal face to face, there is a strong presumption the seller intends to contract with the person physically present, so the contract is voidable (not void) for fraud, and a good-faith third-party buyer can get good title before rescission. If the dealing is in writing or at a distance, identity is fixed by the document, so the contract is void for mistake where the rogue is not the named party — and because it is void, no title can ever pass to a later innocent third party.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that a contract formed in a written hire-purchase agreement, where a rogue impersonates a named third party, is void rather than merely voidable, following Shogun Finance v Hudson?
interaction.explanation: Shogun Finance treats written contracts as fixing identity by reference to the named party on the document. Because the finance company intended to contract only with that named person, and not with the rogue, the contract is void for mistake — a materially harsher result for any later innocent purchaser than the face-to-face cases produce.

parts.heading: Sorting a genuine mistake claim from an ordinary bad deal
parts.voice: comparative — contrasts paired scenarios to sharpen the boundary
body: By this point the shape of the whole topic should be visible: mistake is not a general escape route from a contract that turns out badly. Each branch — common, unilateral, and mistaken identity — has a narrow, specific trigger, and the most common exam error is treating an ordinary disappointing bargain as though it were one of these doctrines.

Compare two buyers of a painting. Buyer One and the seller both believe, wrongly, that the painting is by a minor artist, and price it accordingly; it later turns out to be a significant work worth far more. That is a shared false assumption about quality — exactly Bell v Lever Bros territory, and on the narrow post-Great Peace test, it almost certainly is not fundamental enough to void the sale: the parties got the painting they thought they were buying, just one that turned out to be worth more.

Buyer Two agrees a price with a seller for the same painting during a phone call, then receives a written confirmation with a price a tenth of what was discussed, obviously a typing slip given the earlier call, and rushes to accept before the seller notices. That is Hartog territory: a unilateral mistake as to price, known to the other party, and no contract forms on those mistaken terms at all.

The examiner's fact pattern will rarely announce which doctrine is in play. What distinguishes the two buyers above is not the subject matter (identical painting, both times) but the structure of the mistake — shared or one-sided, about background quality or about an actual term, and whether the other party had the knowledge the doctrine requires. Ask those questions in that order, and the right doctrine, and the right answer, tend to fall out on their own.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often label any fact pattern involving a false belief as 'mistake' and then reach for whichever case they remember best, rather than checking which of the three narrow doctrines the facts actually fit.
components.whyItsWrong: Common mistake, unilateral mistake as to terms, and mistaken identity each have distinct, narrow triggers. A shared but non-fundamental false belief about quality (Bell v Lever Bros, Great Peace), a genuine mistaken assumption not about a term at all, and an ordinary bad bargain are all, in the end, not legal mistakes — and mislabelling the doctrine usually means reaching the wrong remedy, or wrongly concluding a contract is void when it is merely a disappointing one.

interaction.prompt: Which of these is the stronger candidate for an operative mistake, rather than simply a bad bargain?
interaction.scenarioA: A buyer purchases a plot of land believing, along with the seller, that it has planning permission for housing; in fact permission was refused years earlier and neither party checked before contracting.
interaction.scenarioB: A supplier's written order confirmation quotes '£12 per unit' when the parties had just agreed '£120 per unit' on a recorded call minutes earlier, and the buyer immediately emails back accepting at the lower figure before the supplier can respond.
interaction.explanation: B is a unilateral mistake as to a term (price), with the buyer's knowledge fixed by the immediately preceding call — squarely within Hartog. A is a shared mistaken assumption about the land's status, which affects its value and usefulness but does not make the land itself an essentially different thing — after Great Peace, that falls well short of the threshold for common mistake.

testPool.prompt: State the test for common mistake as to quality confirmed in Great Peace Shipping v Tsavliris.
acceptableAnswers: mistake must make the subject matter essentially and radically different from what the parties believed
fundamental mistake rendering the subject matter essentially different
testPool.modelAnswer: The mistake must be sufficiently fundamental to render the subject matter of the contract essentially and radically different from what the parties believed it to be — a merely worse bargain is not enough.

testPool.prompt: What did the House of Lords decide in Bell v Lever Bros about the severance agreement?
options: It remained valid — the mistake made it a worse bargain, not an essentially different one
It was void — the mistake was fundamental enough to void the contract entirely

testPool.prompt: Which of the following best distinguishes unilateral mistake as to a term from a mistaken assumption relevant to common mistake?
options: Unilateral mistake concerns a mistake as to an actual term of the contract (such as price), known or apparent to the other party, whereas common mistake concerns a shared false belief about a background fact
Unilateral mistake can never void a contract, while common mistake regularly does
There is no meaningful distinction; both are assessed under exactly the same legal test
testPool.trapExplanation: Students often collapse the two because both involve a false belief, but the trigger and test differ sharply: unilateral mistake needs the other party's knowledge of a mistake about a term itself; common mistake needs a shared, fundamental mistake about the subject matter, and is in fact the doctrine that almost never succeeds today, not unilateral mistake.

testPool.prompt: In this passage on Hartog v Colin & Shields, highlight the sentence stating the operative principle.
testPool.passage: The seller had quoted hare skins per pound rather than per piece, a figure roughly a third of the intended price, wildly inconsistent with trade practice and the parties' earlier discussions. A party cannot snap up an offer it knows, or must be taken to have known, does not represent the other party's real intention. The buyer's purported acceptance therefore did not create a binding contract at the mistaken price.
testPool.ratioSentence: A party cannot snap up an offer it knows, or must be taken to have known, does not represent the other party's real intention.

testPool.prompt: Order the reasoning steps a court follows in a written-dealing mistaken identity case, following Shogun Finance v Hudson.
items: Identify the party named on the written contract document
Ask whether the finance company intended to contract only with that named party
Conclude the rogue, not being that party, could not have contracted
Hold the contract void for mistake, so no title can pass to a later innocent third party

testPool.prompt: A rogue impersonates someone else while negotiating face to face with a seller, who later discovers the fraud after the goods have already been sold on to a good-faith third party. How confident are you that the original contract with the rogue is void (rather than voidable) on these facts?
testPool.explanation: Face-to-face dealings carry a strong presumption that the seller intends to deal with the person physically present. The contract with the rogue is voidable for fraud, not void, so a good-faith third party who buys before rescission can acquire good title.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario is the stronger candidate for a void contract under the mistaken identity doctrine?
testPool.scenarioA: A rogue walks into a jeweller's shop, claims to be a well-known collector, and persuades the jeweller to accept a cheque and hand over a watch on the spot.
testPool.scenarioB: A rogue completes an online hire-purchase application using a stolen identity document, and a finance company approves the agreement in the real person's name without ever meeting anyone in person.
testPool.explanation: B is a written, distance dealing, where identity is fixed by the named party on the document — squarely Shogun Finance territory, pointing towards a void contract. A is face to face, carrying the strong presumption of intent to deal with the person present, so it is more likely voidable only.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that most directly supports treating this as a unilateral mistake as to a term, rather than a mere bad bargain.
testPool.scenarioText: A wholesaler intends to offer surplus stock at £50 per crate but, due to a spreadsheet error, the emailed price list states £5 per crate. A regular customer, who has bought identical crates from the same wholesaler at £50 every month for two years, places a large order at £5 within minutes of receiving the list.
tappableSpans: emailed price list states £5 per crate
bought identical crates from the same wholesaler at £50 every month for two years
places a large order at £5 within minutes
testPool.correctSpan: bought identical crates from the same wholesaler at £50 every month for two years
testPool.explanation: The customer's own established history with this exact price is what fixes them with knowledge that £5 must be a slip — the objective-knowledge element that Hartog requires, not simply the existence of the error itself.

testPool.prompt: Applying Smith v Hughes, a seller privately hopes a buyer is agreeing to buy old oats when in fact the written contract, reasonably read, describes new oats, and the buyer had no way of knowing the seller meant something different. Is the seller bound by a contract for new oats?
options: Yes — the seller's outward conduct reasonably conveyed agreement to new oats, and undisclosed private intention is irrelevant
No — a party's true private intention always governs regardless of how the contract reads
testPool.explanation: Smith v Hughes applies an objective test: what matters is what a reasonable person would understand from the words and conduct used, not what the seller secretly meant. Since the buyer had no basis to know of any different intention, the contract is read as it reasonably appears.

testPool.prompt: Two collectors buy a vase at auction, both believing it to be an 18th-century original; it is later shown to be a well-made 20th-century reproduction, worth a fraction of the price paid, though visually and functionally the same object either party believed they were buying. Applying Great Peace, is the sale contract void for common mistake?
options: Almost certainly not — the mistake affects value, not the essential character of the thing sold
Yes — any mistake shared by both parties about authenticity automatically voids the contract
testPool.explanation: After Great Peace, the mistake must render the subject matter essentially and radically different in kind, not merely less valuable. A reproduction that is otherwise the same physical object as believed is a hard case for common mistake, and on these facts the claim is very likely to fail — a classic bad bargain rather than an operative mistake.

testPool.prompt: During a phone call, a landscaper and a client agree a price of '£3,000' for garden works. The landscaper's follow-up written quotation, sent an hour later, mistakenly states '£300' due to a formatting error in the document template. The client, who was on the call and clearly heard '£3,000,' emails back the same afternoon purporting to accept the written quotation 'as sent.' Analyse whether a binding contract exists at £300.
factsToOrder: The parties orally agree £3,000 on the phone
The client was on the call and heard the correct figure
The client purports to accept the written figure the same afternoon

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the client can hold the landscaper to a contract at £300, given the client's knowledge of the figure actually agreed.
modelAnswer.rule: Under Hartog v Colin & Shields and the objective test in Smith v Hughes, a party cannot snap up an offer it knows, or must reasonably be taken to have known, does not reflect the other party's real intention; no contract forms on the mistaken term.
modelAnswer.application: The client's own presence on the earlier call, where £3,000 was clearly agreed, fixes them with actual knowledge that the written £300 figure is a slip. A reasonable person in the client's position could not genuinely believe the landscaper intended to reduce the price by a factor of ten within the hour.
modelAnswer.conclusion: No binding contract exists at £300; this is a unilateral mistake as to a term known to the other party, and the purported acceptance cannot create a contract on those terms.

testPool.prompt: In Shogun Finance v Hudson, why did the innocent purchaser of the car from the rogue not acquire good title?
options: Because the original hire-purchase contract was void for mistake, meaning the rogue never had title to pass on
Because the innocent purchaser had failed to check the car's registration documents

testPool.prompt: Which scenario better illustrates the narrow surviving scope of common mistake after Great Peace, rather than a doctrine that has effectively disappeared?
testPool.scenarioA: Both parties contract for the sale of specific goods that, unknown to either, had already been destroyed by fire before the contract was made, so there was nothing capable of being sold at all.
testPool.scenarioB: Both parties contract for the sale of a used car that turns out to need more repairs than either expected, making it a worse purchase than anticipated.
testPool.explanation: A concerns the non-existence of the subject matter altogether — there is nothing left for the contract to attach to, which is the paradigm surviving case for common mistake voiding a contract. B is a classic bad bargain: the car is still the car both parties thought they were buying, merely in worse condition than hoped, which Great Peace treats as insufficient.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common error in this lesson's test items is applying 'mistake' as a general label for any false belief, rather than checking whether the facts fit one of the three narrow triggers — common mistake as to a fundamental fact, unilateral mistake as to a term known to the other party, or mistaken identity under the correct face-to-face/written framework.
